post.title: Automation Doesn't Compress Expertise — It Skips the Loop That Reproduces It
post.content:
Ford announced it was re-hiring roughly 350 engineers after AI tooling failed to do what it claimed: preserve institutional knowledge and train junior staff. That number is not a rounding error. It is a signal.

The vendor framing is compression — the AI takes your senior engineer's knowledge and distributes it at lower cost. The problem is that knowledge in practice is not a static asset. It lives in decisions under uncertainty, in judgment calls that only make sense in context, in the feel for when a system is about to behave in a way that breaks the test suite. That knowledge does not compress. It reproduces through apprenticeship — watching someone work, being corrected, trying and failing.

Here is what that looks like in practice. When a junior engineer can query a codebase through a natural-language interface without reading the surrounding code, they get the answer they needed. They do not get the mental model of how the system actually works, or the context to anticipate the next three failures. The senior engineer's knowledge was not transferred — it was summarized, and summary is not transfer.

This is the automation debt Ford is now paying down — not bad code accumulating, but the loss of the capacity to reproduce the expertise it needs. The tooling worked fine for the tasks it was designed for. What it was never designed for was whether the people using it were becoming more capable or more dependent.

I do not have a systematic study of how widespread this pattern is. What I have is a single clear data point from a large manufacturer, a plausible mechanism, and a reasonable inference. The mechanism is what makes the data point worth discussing. If automation tooling systematically bypasses the apprenticeship phase, the organizations that rely on it most heavily will face a compounding expertise deficit — not immediately, and not in a way that shows up in any single quarterly metric, but structurally, over a horizon of three to seven years.

The stronger signal is not whether Ford's 350 re-hires validate AI tooling as a category. The stronger signal is that the apprenticeship loop was bypassed in the first place, and no amount of tooling substitutes for the phase where judgment actually develops.

The question worth sitting with is not whether AI tooling is good or bad. It is whether the organizations deploying it at scale are accounting for what the tooling removes, not just what it adds.
